Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
The event happened because of the way I acted
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Marisol, a 27-year-old Latin American animator, came to therapy months after a relationship she had once described as intense and affectionate had ended in violence. Her ex-boyfriend had begun with apologies and charm, then escalated into control that made her feel small in her own apartment, until one night he struck her during an argument and left her shaking on the kitchen floor, stunned by how quickly the person she loved had become frightening. What stayed with Marisol was not only the pain of that night but the sense that she had been changed by it in some permanent way. In the days that followed, she kept telling herself that she was not the same person who used to joke with coworkers at her studio, sketch late into the night, or trust easily. She described feeling “damaged,” as if something in her had been bent out of shape and could not be fully repaired.

As she replayed the relationship, Marisol turned the blame inward. She became preoccupied with the idea that the abuse had happened because of the way she had acted: because she had answered back, because she had stayed too long, because she had ignored small warning signs and tried to smooth things over. She spoke with shame about moments when she had apologized to him after he hurt her, or kept the peace rather than confronting him, and said those memories now felt like evidence against her own judgment. What hurt her most was the sense that she had acted against the values she had grown up with. In her family, she had always seen herself as loyal, warm, and careful not to harm others, yet in the relationship she found herself lying to friends about bruises, making excuses, and shrinking around him to avoid conflict. She experienced that not as a simple mistake but as a betrayal of who she believed herself to be.

Over the months after the breakup, Marisol’s world narrowed around these beliefs. At work, where she spent long hours in a bright studio surrounded by screens and storyboards, she noticed herself flinching when a colleague approached too quickly or when someone’s tone sharpened in a meeting. Even ordinary feedback from her supervisor could send her mind back to the bedroom door slamming or to the kitchen where the assault had happened, and she would go quiet, convinced that her body and confidence had been permanently altered. She began spending more time alone after work, turning down invitations from friends and leaving social events early, partly because she did not want to answer questions and partly because being around other people made her feel exposed in the ways she now feared most. The more she withdrew, the more certain she became that the relationship had left a lasting mark on her, and that everyone could somehow see the change even if they did not say it.

Her self-blame kept returning in private, especially at night when the apartment was still. She would remember the arguments, her own attempts to keep him calm, and the moments when she thought she should have left sooner. Those memories fed the belief that the violence had happened because she had not acted correctly, and that belief made it harder for her to see herself as worthy of kindness or protection. It also deepened her shame about the ways she had compromised her own values to survive the relationship. She described feeling trapped between disgust at what had happened and a harsh conviction that she had somehow helped make it possible, which left her stuck in a quieter, more isolated version of herself.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was still working, but only by forcing herself through the day and then collapsing at home. She said she was finally coming in because she could no longer bear the thought that this permanent damage was simply who she was now. What she feared most was that she had become someone weak, careless, and unlike the woman she had been, though a small part of her still hoped therapy might help her separate what happened to her from who she is.
